title: Merge or rebase?
explanation:
There are two ways to bring one branch's work into another.

**Merge.** `git merge topic` (run on the receiving branch). If the receiving branch hasn't moved since `topic` split off, Git just moves the pointer forward — a **fast-forward**, no new commit. If both sides have new commits, Git performs a three-way merge of the two tips and their common ancestor and records a **merge commit** with two parents. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible, so the branch stays visible in history.

**Rebase.** `git rebase trunk` (run on `topic`) takes the commits unique to `topic` and **replays** them, one by one, on top of `trunk`. The result is a straight line, and `trunk` can then fast-forward to include it. The final snapshot is the same as with a merge — only the history differs.

```bash
git switch trunk && git merge --no-ff topic   # keep a merge commit
git switch topic && git rebase trunk          # or: replay topic onto trunk for linear history
```

Rebasing creates *new* commits with new ids. The rule: **do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.** Rebase your private work freely; merge shared work.
keyIdeas: Fast-forward: the pointer just moves; no merge commit.
Three-way merge of diverged branches creates a merge commit; `--no-ff` always creates one.
Rebase replays your unique commits on top of another branch: linear history, new commit ids.
Never rebase commits others may have based work on.

workedExample.problem: `trunk` and a branch `bakery` have both gained a commit since they split. Integrate `bakery` into `trunk` in two ways and compare: (a) merge, and (b) rebase `bakery` onto `trunk`, then fast-forward.
steps: (a) On `trunk`, `git merge bakery -m 'Merge bakery'` must combine two diverged tips, so Git creates a merge commit with two parents.
(b) In a second copy, on `bakery` run `git rebase trunk`: bakery's commit is replayed on top of trunk's new commit, getting a new id.
Then on `trunk`, `git merge --ff-only bakery` succeeds because `trunk` is now an ancestor of `bakery` — history is a straight line.
Both approaches end with the same files; only the shape of history differs.

Run it in a throwaway folder:
```sh
git init -q -b trunk base && cd base
printf 'tea\n' > menu.md && git add menu.md && git commit -q -m 'Add menu'
git switch -q -c bakery && printf 'scones\n' > bakery.md && git add bakery.md && git commit -q -m 'Add bakery'
git switch -q trunk && printf 'tea 3\n' > prices.md && git add prices.md && git commit -q -m 'Add prices'
cd .. && git clone -q base merged && git clone -q base rebased
cd merged && git switch -q bakery && git switch -q trunk
git merge -q bakery -m 'Merge bakery'
[ "$(git rev-list --parents -n 1 HEAD | wc -w)" -eq 3 ]      # merge commit: itself + two parents
cd ../rebased && git switch -q bakery && old=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git rebase -q trunk
[ "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" != "$old" ]   # replayed as a new commit
git switch -q trunk && git merge -q --ff-only bakery
[ "$(git rev-list --merges --count HEAD)" -eq 0 ]           # linear: no merge commits
[ "$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree})" = "$(cd ../merged && git rev-parse HEAD^{tree})" ]   # same snapshot
echo ok
```
workedExample.answer: Merging creates a two-parent merge commit; rebasing replays `Add bakery` as a new commit on top of `Add prices` so `trunk` fast-forwards with no merge commit. Both end with identical files (the same tree).

pitfalls: Rebasing a branch teammates already pulled, so their history no longer matches yours.
Expecting `git merge` to always create a merge commit — it fast-forwards when it can unless you pass `--no-ff`.
Running the command on the wrong branch: you merge *into* the branch you're on, and rebase the branch you're on *onto* another.

citations.quote: With --ff, when possible resolve the merge as a fast-forward (only update the branch pointer to match the merged branch; do not create a merge commit).
With --no-ff, create a merge commit in all cases, even when the merge could instead be resolved as a fast-forward.
It performs a three-way merge between the two latest branch snapshots (C3 and C4) and the most recent common ancestor of the two (C2), creating a new snapshot (and commit).
With the rebase command, you can take all the changes that were committed on one branch and replay them on a different branch.
whether it's the last of the rebased commits for a rebase or the final merge commit after a merge, is the same snapshot — it's only the history that is different.
the branches to be merged must be tied together by a merge commit that has both of them as its parents.
At this point, you can go back to the master branch and do a fast-forward merge.
Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.
When you rebase stuff, you're abandoning existing commits and creating new ones that are similar but different.
